record.paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
record.original_question: Do interatomic zero-flux surfaces act as holograms for topological atoms by encoding the right amount of information needed to deduce basin properties from boundary data, rather than requiring full three-dimensional property densities inside each atomic basin?

evidence.quote: 2.4. Do the interatomic-surfaces act as “hologram” for the topological atoms?
In this context, it is possible to demonstrate that to determine many properties of the topological atoms just knowing what goes on the interatomic-surfaces suffices.

Therefore, the considered example is not something exceptional and the subsystem hypervirial theorem also entails the same type of the relationship between the “bulk” and the “boundary” of a topological atom and one may claim that just knowing the currents at the boundaries is enough to deduce the basin properties.
All these are in line with the idea that the inter-atomic surfaces may be act as holograms, i.e. coding the right amount

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $\rho:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be the (smooth) one-electron density of a molecular system, and let $\nabla\rho$ denote its gradient field. A topological atom (or atomic basin) $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ is a maximal open region whose points all flow, under the gradient dynamical system $\dot{\mathbf r}=\nabla\rho(\mathbf r)$, to the same nuclear attractor. The boundary $\partial\Omega$ consists of interatomic zero-flux surfaces, characterized by
$$\nabla\rho(\mathbf r)\cdot \mathbf n(\mathbf r)=0\qquad\text{for all }\mathbf r\in\partial\Omega,$$
where $\mathbf n$ is the outward unit normal. For a quantum-mechanical observable represented by an operator $\hat A$, the associated basin property is the integral
$$A(\Omega)=\int_\Omega a(\mathbf r)\,d\mathbf r,$$
where $a(\mathbf r)$ is the corresponding (real-space) property density derived from the underlying many-electron wavefunction. The subsystem hypervirial theorem expresses certain such basin properties as fluxes of associated current densities $\mathbf j_A$ across $\partial\Omega$:
$$A(\Omega)=\oint_{\partial\Omega} \mathbf j_A(\mathbf r)\cdot \mathbf n(\mathbf r)\,dS.$$

Problem. Establish (or refute) the following "holographic" principle for topological atoms: prove a general Gauss-type theorem asserting that, for every physically admissible quantum-mechanical observable $\hat A$, the basin property $A(\Omega)$ is fully determined by data supported on the two-dimensional interatomic boundary $\partial\Omega$ (e.g.\ by suitable surface densities, currents, or boundary functionals derived from the wavefunction), without requiring knowledge of the three-dimensional property density $a(\mathbf r)$ throughout the interior of $\Omega$. Equivalently, characterize precisely the class of observables for which such a boundary-to-bulk reduction holds, and determine whether it extends to all observables relevant to the quantum theory of atoms in molecules.
artifact.status_search_result: The "hologram" idea for interatomic zero-flux surfaces is supported only partially via the subsystem hypervirial theorem. Reviews of QTAIM foundations explicitly state that a general Gauss-like theorem covering all conceivable properties of topological atoms is still needed, and that a boundary-only theory yielding all basin properties has not been derived. Hence the problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
status_evidence.snippet: To generally support the hologram idea, a general Gauss-like theorem for topological atoms is needed that goes beyond the subsystem hypervirial theorem and covers all conceivable properties of the topological atoms.
status_evidence.claim: A general boundary-to-bulk theorem for all basin properties has not yet been established; only special cases via the hypervirial theorem are known.

status_evidence.title: Non-covalent interactions from a Quantum Chemical Topology perspective
status_evidence.snippet: Discussion of QTAIM foundations and interatomic surfaces as defining zero-flux boundaries of atomic basins, with ongoing research into properties derivable from these surfaces.
status_evidence.claim: Recent QTAIM literature continues to investigate boundary-derived basin properties without claiming a complete holographic reduction.
